stem: Why is τ=J^TK_x(X_d−X) not, by itself, the complete Cartesian model-based decoupling law developed later?

options.text: The later law replaces J^T by J^−1 to convert Cartesian force to torque.
It contains virtual stiffness feedback but omits the Cartesian inertia scaling, velocity/gravity compensation and desired-acceleration servo structure.
It cannot produce a joint torque because J^T is reserved exclusively for velocity mapping.
It already cancels all nonlinear dynamics simply because the error is Cartesian.

stem: At one instant, X_d=[1,2]ᵀ m, X=[0.5,2.5]ᵀ m, Ẋ_d=[0.8,−0.2]ᵀ m/s, Ẋ=[0.3,0.3]ᵀ m/s and Ẍ_d=[1,2]ᵀ m/s². With K_p=diag(4,6) s⁻², K_v=diag(2,4) s⁻¹, M_x=[[2,1],[1,3]] kg, V_x+G_x=[1,2]ᵀ N and J=[[1,2],[0,1]] m/rad, what torque follows from u=Ẍ_d+K_v(Ẋ_d−Ẋ)+K_p(X_d−X), F=M_xu+V_x+G_x and τ=J^TF?
assumptions: This is an explicitly supplied translation-only instantaneous example with two revolute actuators, compatible frames and no saturation.
The desired-minus-actual error convention is used; the Jacobian and dynamics correspond to the actual configuration.

stem: On a smooth desired inverse-kinematics branch, let J=[[1,2],[0,1]] m/rad and its total time derivative J̇=[[0,1],[1,0]] m/(rad·s). For Ẋ_d=[3,1]ᵀ m/s and Ẍ_d=[2,4]ᵀ m/s², what desired joint acceleration follows from Ẋ_d=Jθ̇_d and Ẍ_d=Jθ̈_d+J̇θ̇_d?

assumptions: The 2×2 Jacobian is nonsingular at this instant, and all task vectors use the same translation frame.
J and J̇ are evaluated along the selected desired branch; J̇ is supplied as the total derivative along that branch, not a matrix inverse of a derivative.
